newsitem.title: USA: Motorola Q3 EPS may be down 25 pct vs Q2.
newsitem.headline: Motorola Q3 EPS may be down 25 pct vs Q2.

text.p: Motorola Inc said Wednesday that its projection of a potential "significant drop" in third quarter earnings compared with the second quarter could mean a decline of 25 percent or more.
In a conference call, Motorola did not specify the amount of decline likely in third quarter earnings compared with the $0.54 a share it earned in the second quarter.
But Edward Gams, vice president and director of investor relations, said Motorola normally uses the term "significant" to describe a change of 25 percent or more.
According to First Call, the consensus of analysts' estimates for the third quarter was $0.50 a share.
In a statement issued earlier, Motorola blamed the weaker earnings outlook in particular on its semiconductor business.
Gams declined to give further specific details on its third quarter outlook, pending results from September sales.

But looking ahead, he said Motorola is hopeful that the semiconductor industry will return to a "growth mode" in 1997. The company does not expect, however, a "sharp renewal" of industry growth next year.
"And we're hopeful that signs of that improving situation in semiconductors will emerge during the fourth quarter," Gams said.
He added that the commercialization of the personal communications systems, or PCS, in the United States will benefit Motorola's cellular business in 1997.
In the third quarter, Gams said, the weakness in earnings is linked to subscriber equipment in cellular telephones and pagers, not in infrastructure for those systems.
"It is pagers and cellular phones subscriber equipment in each case that is causing us to see these results," Gams said.
Gams said he expects Motorola's worldwide market share for cellular handsets will decline this year compared with 1995.

"It did drop in 1995 versus 1994 by a few percentage points, and will very likely do so again this year," Gams said. "The primary reason for that decline is going to be in the international markets. Japan is a very large factor in that."

He added that Motorola likely will see a decline in international market share for GSM, or global system of mobile communications. Gams said Motorola hopes to recoup some of that lost market share through new digital cellular products.
Asked by an analyst why Motorola previewed its earnings, which is not its typical policy, Gams cited the shortfall in second quarter earnings.
In the second quarter, Motorola's $0.54 a share in earnings compared with a $0.79 in the 1995 period and analysts' expectations at that time of $0.68.

"As we saw a similar situation was developing here in the third quarter, we felt that the present set of circumstances was really quite unique for us relative to the company's performance over a number of years, and that it warranted a communication to investors at this time," Gams said.
